entities.name: Pashupatinath Temple
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Pashupatinath Temple in Kathmandu, Nepal, on the banks of the Bagmati River, is the most sacred Hindu temple in the world for Shaivites — devotees of Shiva — and the most important religious site in Nepal. Dedicated to Pashupatinath (Lord of All Animals), an aspect of Shiva, the temple complex dates in its current form to the 5th century CE (though the site's religious significance extends much earlier), and the main pagoda-style shikhara was rebuilt in the 17th century. UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1979.

Pashupatinath is Nepal's most important pilgrimage site, drawing hundreds of thousands of Hindu pilgrims annually, particularly during Maha Shivaratri (Shiva's great night) when over a million devotees gather from across South Asia. The complex includes the main two-storied pagoda temple (non-Hindus not admitted inside), cremation ghats on the Bagmati River where Hindus are cremated and their ashes consigned to the river flowing to the Ganges, and a vast complex of smaller temples, ashrams, and shrines.

The Bagmati River ghats at Pashupatinath are one of the most spiritually charged sites in Hinduism: open-air cremations are performed continuously, and dying Hindus from across Nepal and India are brought to spend their final hours near the temple. The site's philosophical centrality to the Hindu understanding of life, death, and moksha (liberation) makes it one of the most profound living religious complexes in the world. UNESCO protection and its status as Nepal's national religious symbol make it central to Nepali national identity.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Pashupatinath Temple — Nepal's most sacred site, the world's premier Shaivite pilgrimage destination, a living site of Hindu last rites philosophy, and a UNESCO World Heritage site — is one of Hinduism's most spiritually and culturally significant living religious complexes.
